newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Roadway sees growth opportunities.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Roadway sees growth opportunities.

text.p: Roadway Express Inc sees only modest revenue growth in 1997, though officials at Akron, Ohio-based trucking company have spotted opportunities in expanding services and moving into markets outside the United States.
"We are, right now, not looking for a tremendous amount of revenue growth," President Michael Wickham said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday. He did not provide a specific forecast.
Roadway generated 1996 revenues of $2.4 billion versus $2.3 billion in 1995.
Wickham said Roadway would seek to make further efficiencies after last year cutting the number of terminals it operates.
Roadway, which was spun off from Caliber System Inc a year ago, reported 1996 earnings of $1.07 a share versus a 1995 net loss of $0.62.
The stock closed up 1-3/4 at 22-7/8 on the Nasdaq.

Chief Financial Officer Dawson Cunningham said Roadway was concentrating on its core less-than-truckload carrier business, but new higher-profit "expedited services" and overseas service could hold opportunities for the company.
Earlier, Cunningham said 1997 earnings growth would meet most analysts' forecasts.

Faster-than-standard delivery and exclusive service, where equipment is dedicated to a single customer, were introduced on a pilot basis this fall, he said. Wickham said the company would offer those services systemwide this year.
Shipping containers overseas accounted for about five percent of 1996 revenues, said Wickham, who is also chief executive officer.
"I think this year (the international business) grew at about 20 percent or a little bit better," he said. "We should be able to maintain that kind of growth on international."
Roadway's staff and information systems facilitate overseas shipping for customers, including small companies, he said.
Responding to queries about union drivers, Wickham said experienced drivers have fewer accidents and higher productivity than less-experienced drivers.
"Our excellent safety record mitigates some of the higher costs attached to wages and benefits," he said. "It's not quite (offsetting) but it's close."
Roadway is still working to regain business lost to non-union companies in a 1994 strike, he said.
